item.title: Check Point CVE-2026-16232 Exploited, RefluXFS Root Flaw, and Chaos msaRAT Emerge
item.content:encoded:
Check Point Patches Exploited SmartConsole Flaw Allowing Full Admin Access — Must Read

Check Point released urgent fixes for actively exploited SmartConsole and management server flaws, including a critical authentication bypass that can give remote attackers full administrative access when management interfaces are exposed to the internet without Trusted Client restrictions. Customers should apply the July 22 Jumbo hotfix and restrict management access to trusted IPs immediately.

  • Check Point released security updates for vulnerabilities affecting Security Management and Multi-Domain Management products, including a critical flaw that is being actively exploited.
  • CVE-2026-16232 is an authentication bypass in the Check Point SmartConsole login process that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to obtain an application login token and authenticate with full administrative privileges.
  • Check Point said the exploited flaw affects a very specific configuration where Management is exposed directly to the internet without IP restrictions.
  • The updates also address CVE-2026-62144, which can allow unauthenticated remote attackers to execute administrative commands, and CVE-2026-62145, which can allow a read-only Gaia Portal user to execute commands with root privileges.
  • CISA added CVE-2026-16232 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and required Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to apply fixes by July 25, 2026.

Nine-Year-Old RefluXFS Linux Flaw Gives Local Users Root on Default RHEL Installs — Must Read

A nine-year-old Linux kernel flaw in XFS reflink handling, CVE-2026-64600 “RefluXFS,” can let local unprivileged users overwrite root-owned files and gain persistent root on affected default RHEL-family, Fedora Server, and Amazon Linux installs. Administrators should install the fixed kernel and reboot, as there is no practical mitigation once an XFS filesystem was created with reflink enabled.

  • RefluXFS, tracked as CVE-2026-64600, is a Linux kernel flaw disclosed on July 22 that lets an unprivileged local user overwrite root-owned files on an XFS filesystem and gain persistent root access.
  • Qualys said default installations of Red Hat Enterprise Linux and its derivatives, Fedora Server, and Amazon Linux can meet the conditions for exploitation when XFS was created with reflink enabled.
  • Exploitation requires Linux 4.11 or later without the RefluXFS fix, an XFS filesystem created with reflink=1, and a readable target plus an attacker-writable directory on the same XFS filesystem.
  • The upstream fix was merged on July 16, and vendors including Red Hat and Debian have begun shipping backported kernel updates for affected releases.
  • Qualys said there is no practical mitigation or temporary configuration change, so systems must install the vendor kernel update and reboot to run the fixed kernel.

New msaRAT malware uses Chrome, Edge browsers to route C2 traffic — Should Read

The Chaos ransomware gang is using a new Rust backdoor called msaRAT that hides its command-and-control traffic by controlling headless Chrome or Edge through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Its use of Cloudflare Workers, WebRTC, and Twilio TURN relays makes the attacker infrastructure harder to detect and trace.

  • The Chaos ransomware gang is using a new Rust-based backdoor called msaRAT that routes command-and-control communication through Chrome or Edge browsers.
  • Cisco Talos observed recent Chaos ransomware attacks that began with email or voice phishing and continued with remote management software used for persistence.
  • Attackers downloaded an MSI installer posing as a Windows update, which loaded msaRAT as lib.dll directly in system memory.
  • msaRAT launches Chrome or Microsoft Edge in headless mode, enables the browser’s remote debugging interface, and uses the Chrome DevTools Protocol to inject JavaScript into a new browser tab.
  • The malware uses Cloudflare Workers, WebRTC, Twilio TURN servers, and two layers of encryption to hide the attacker’s server and make the traffic look like normal web activity.

Microsoft working to fix Exchange Online mailbox quarantine issue — Should Read

Microsoft is working to fix an Exchange Online incident that has incorrectly quarantined some mailboxes, preventing affected users from sending or receiving email and accessing calendars. The issue was caused by a recent infrastructure change that led to excessive memory consumption, and Microsoft is still cleaning up indexing data to restore service.

  • Microsoft is working to resolve an Exchange Online issue, tracked as EX1436407, that has been incorrectly quarantining some customers' mailboxes since July 19.
  • Affected Exchange Online users may have trouble receiving and sending emails and accessing their calendars, while senders may receive non-delivery reports when emailing quarantined mailboxes.
  • Microsoft said a recent infrastructure change caused excessive memory consumption from unexpected indexing data, leading to an out-of-memory condition that incorrectly quarantined mailboxes.
  • Microsoft identified the incident as a recurrence of a previous issue tracked as EX1434354 and said additional remediation steps were required for full restoration.
  • Microsoft reported that cleanup of excess indexing data had progressed from 66% to 72% complete on Wednesday, but it had not yet provided a timeline for full remediation.
